title: Dawadawa
localName: Dawadawa — dori, koligu, fermented locust bean
author: Northern Ghanaian tradition
desc: An alkaline fermentation — the pH rises to 8.1 or higher and the finished seeds are sticky, pungent and covered with a greyish mucilaginous layer.
longDesc: Dawadawa is fermented African locust bean and it is the deepest savoury note in West African cooking. Crucially it is an ALKALINE fermentation: where a souring goes acid, this goes basic, with the pH rising from near neutral to 8.1 or higher as protein breaks down to amino acids and ammonia. Seeds are boiled twelve to twenty-four hours to soften the hard testa, de-hulled, boiled again, then wrapped and left two to four days at ambient temperature. The endpoint is visible and smellable: sticky, pungent, covered with a greyish mucilaginous layer. Every Ghanaian source consulted gave a time with no cue; the usable endpoint is Nigerian and labelled as such.
ingredients: Wood ash, for the pounding stage in the Ghanaian method
Water, for repeated boiling and washing
// Jute bags or banana leaves, for the fermentation
// No household quantities are published. See the note.
steps: Dry and sort the locust bean seeds.
Boil them 12 to 24 hours, to soften the hard testa.
Pound with wood ash in a mortar, then wash repeatedly to remove the broken testa.
Boil the kernels again — about an hour in the documented endpoint source, two to four hours in the Ghanaian accounts.
Drain, and place in a fabric bag weighted to press away excess water, or wrap in banana leaves.
Ferment 2 to 4 days at ambient temperature.

// ENDPOINT: the pH rises from near neutral to 8.1 or higher. The seeds become sticky with a strong ammoniacal smell, and the colour changes from light brown to dark brown under a greyish mucilaginous layer.
// This endpoint is documented for Nigerian practice; every Ghanaian source consulted gives a time without a cue. See the note.
chefTips: It is an ALKALINE fermentation and that is the thing to understand. Proper dawadawa goes basic, to pH 8.1 or above; a souring means something has gone wrong.
The endpoint is a smell and a surface: strong ammoniacal, sticky, with a greyish mucilaginous layer, and the colour shifting from light brown to dark brown.
Twelve to twenty-four hours of boiling at the start sounds absurd and is correct — the testa on a locust bean seed is extremely hard.
Wood ash in the pounding stage is the Ghanaian documented practice. Wood ash is genuinely alkaline, which presumably helps set the fermentation's direction.
A consumer survey found that good quality dawadawa has a strong ammonia-like smell and a dark brown colour. That is the market test.
Temperature rises during the ferment — from about 30 degrees to a maximum of about 50 in twenty-four hours, by one cited account. That self-heating is a sign it is working.
Only women produce dawadawa, by one organisation's account of the Ghanaian practice. Use it by the tablespoon: two tablespoons seasons a whole soup.
commonMistakes: Expecting it to sour rather than go alkaline.
Cutting the initial boil short, leaving the testa intact.
Skipping the repeated washing after pounding.
Fermenting in a sealed container rather than a breathable bag or leaves.
Using too much in a dish — it is extremely potent.
sources: PUBLISHED AS A DOCUMENTED PROCESS, NOT A HOUSEHOLD RECIPE. No source publishes quantities; none have been invented.

A DISCLOSURE THAT COMES FIRST, because it governs this entry: THE FERMENTATION WAS REFUSED FOR EVERY GHANAIAN SOURCE CONSULTED, each of which gives a time with no observable cue. The endpoint published above is documented for NIGERIAN practice and is labelled as such in the step list. This is the same treatment given to banku, whose only sensory cue is Ivorian (GHA041).

THE USABLE ENDPOINT, and the only dawadawa source found anywhere with time plus an observable cue plus a pH: Ugwuanyi J.O. and Okpara A.N., 'Current Status of Alkaline Fermented Foods and Seasoning Agents of Africa', IntechOpen, 2019. THIS IS NOT GHANA — the chapter says the product is 'widely consumed... in the Northern and some part of Southern Nigeria' and cites Okpara & Ugwuanyi (2017) and Achi (2005). Verbatim: 'boiling of the locust bean seeds for 12-24 h, followed by manual de-hulling... boiled again for 1 h'; 'placed in jute bags or wrapped with banana leaves and allowed to ferment for 2-4 days at ambient temperature'; 'the pH increases from near neutral to 8.1 or higher due to the breakdown of protein to amino acids and ammonia'; 'At the end the product is sticky, with pungent odor and covered with mucilaginous grayish layer'.

THE GHANAIAN SOURCES, all REFUSED for lack of a cue, with their figures recorded. (1) Slow Food Foundation, Ark of Taste, organisation byline, 'Last modified April 21, 2020': 'Only women produce dawadawa.' Seeds dried, sorted, boiled in an aluminium pot, then pounded with wood ash in a log mortar. Verbatim: 'The seeds are boiled again for two hours, and then drained and placed in a fabric bag, which is weighted to press away excess water. The seeds are left for 72 hours, until the dawadawa is fully fermented.' REFUSED: 72 h with no sensory or pH cue. A cultural note from one pass: nuha nua herb and red chili are placed on top in transit to ward off spirits. (2) Northern Voices Ghana, byline the blog's own name, 2 July 2016, quoted: 'the locust beans (dori), as it is called among the Dagombas, are first boiled for at least 24 hours... mixed with wood ash and pounded and washed several times... boiled for another 3-4 hours... allowed to ferment for two days. On the third day... transferred to a deep bowl and allowed to ferment for another 24 hours.' REFUSED. NOTE the quoted passage is unattributed and refers to 'the source document', so it is probably copied. (3) Whitby 1968: 'Usually the seeds are boiled for twenty-four hours to soften the hard testa, then pounded and washed to remove broken testa. The kernels are then boiled again, crushed to paste, and set -aside two or three days to ferment.' REFUSED.

NEAR-MISSES, refused strictly: Kareem Arthur in Whetstone Magazine (bio 'a writer from South East London'), whose process wording is near-identical to Slow Food's and is therefore derivative rather than independent — 'left to rest for three days, until the dawadawa is fully fermented producing a sticky fermented mixture.' And Abena Offeh-Gyimah (bio 'a writer, researcher, and poet'): 'boiled twice in order to get them ready for a three day fermentation process', and 'Once it's fermented, it has a sticky and sour taste on its own' — which describes the product rather than stating a test. Also the National Research Council's Lost Crops of Africa Vol. II, 2006: 'After two or three days the odoriferous result is pressed into cakes or balls.' No cue.

THE CITED NIGERIAN LITERATURE THAT CORROBORATES THE ALKALINE READING, quoted inside a Ghanaian thesis — Opai-Tetteh S., 'The Microbial Activities Involved in the Alkaline Fermentation of Soybeans into Dawadawa', University of Ghana MPhil, 1999, citing Odunfa 1983 on AFRICAN LOCUST BEAN: 'The pH increases to about 8.1 during the first 30h of fermentation, due in part to the production of ammonia.' 'The temperature of the fermenting seeds increase from about 30 °C to a maximum of about 50 °C in 24h.' Seeds 'have a greyish sticky mucilage covering and a strong ammoniacal smell. The colour also changes from light brown to dark brown.' Seeds ferment 'for about 36 h or longer', with '3-4 days' mentioned elsewhere. THESE ARE LITERATURE QUOTES INSIDE A GHANAIAN THESIS, not that thesis's own data. Its own measurements are on SOYBEAN, over 72 h: boiled soy pH 6.6 to 8.3, roasted 6.4 to 8.2, titratable acidity 0.1 to 0.4 (SINGLE-PASS). Its consumer survey gives the market test: 'a good quality dawadawa has a strong ammonia-like smell and a dark brown colour.'

FURTHER GHANAIAN WORK, all on SOYBEAN rather than locust bean: Amoa-Awua W.K., Terlabie N.N., Sakyi-Dawson E., 'Screening of 42 Bacillus isolates for ability to ferment soybeans into dawadawa', International Journal of Food Microbiology 106, 2006, TWO-PASS: 'The pH of the samples, which increased from 6.37-6.58 to 8.22-8.85 during fermentation', with Bacillus counts above 10^9 cfu/g; duration and temperature are not in the abstract. And Darkwa S., Amoa-Awua W.K., Sakyi-Dawson E., 2003, abstract only: 'The bacterial population, pH and moisture content increased with fermentation. The titratable acidity increased in the first 24 h and then dropped as fermentation progressed', with amylase activity peaking at 72 h and organisms B. subtilis, B. licheniformis, B. pumilus and B. cereus. NO pH NUMBERS in that one.

A 2025 GHANAIAN PAPER ON REAL LOCUST BEAN, with no usable figures: Golly K.M. et al., 'Microbial Diversity, Nutritional Composition, and Health Implications of Fermented Locust Bean Seed (Dawadawa) From Ghana', International Journal of Food Science 8444101, DOI 10.1155/ijfo/8444101. SINGLE-PASS. It names 'alkaline fermentation' and 'ammoniacal odor' but gives NO pH, NO time and NO temperature.

AND ONE MORE on real Parkia biglobosa: Boateng et al. 2014, KNUST, Livestock Research for Rural Development 26(10): seeds fermented 'in a basket which was covered with jute sacks ... for 4 days'. NO pH reported.

THE REMAINING GAP, named: NO GHANAIAN PAPER WAS FOUND WITH A pH TIME SERIES FROM TRADITIONAL LOCUST-BEAN DAWADAWA. The Ghanaian pH figures are all soybean laboratory work; the locust-bean figures are Nigerian or cited from Nigerian literature. Spoilage-by-acidification is also NOT stated for dawadawa in any Ghanaian source consulted.

A RELATED PAPER WITH NO ENDPOINT: K.B. Pelig-Ba, 'Effect of Ash, KOH and Millet on the Fermentation of Parkia biglobosa Seeds to Form a Condiment', University for Development Studies Navrongo, Pakistan Journal of Nutrition 8(10):1548-1554, 2009. Abstract: 'pH, crude protein, fat and moisture increased during the period of fermentation, while carbohydrate, crude fibre and ash decreased.' Fermentation was six days; the millet-treated sample reached pH 7.68 (SINGLE-PASS). No ash, KOH or millet quantities were obtained and the PDF was not retrievable.

A NAME DISAGREEMENT, unreconciled: Whitby 1968 gives the Dagomba name as 'Koligu' and the species as Parkia clappertoniana; Northern Voices Ghana gives the Dagomba name as 'dori'; Slow Food and Northern Voices both say Parkia biglobosa. Both names and both species attributions are recorded.

DAWADAWA QUANTITIES IN SOURCED RECIPES, for scale: 15 g in the ICLEI ayoyo (GHA074); 2 tablespoons in Adwoa Fofie's ayoyo (GHA073); 2 tablespoons of locust beans in the bito soup (GHA075); 1 teaspoon in a flagged source; 2 teaspoons in the garden egg stew (GHA026); 1 tablespoon of powder in the Ewe palmnut soup (GHA021). NOWHERE IS A RATIO JUSTIFIED.
storage: Months as dried cakes or balls, kept sealed.
reheating: Not applicable. Bloomed in hot oil or added to the pot.
healthBenefits: Fermentation raises free amino acids and B vitamins substantially.
A significant plant protein source in northern Ghanaian diets.
Documented as reducing antinutrients in the raw seed.
Used by the tablespoon, so it contributes flavour rather than calories.
culturalNote: Dawadawa is the ingredient that makes northern Ghanaian soups taste like themselves, and the alkaline fermentation behind it is the same chemistry as natto or Japanese fermented soybean — protein broken down to ammonia rather than sugar to acid. That only women produce it, by one account, and that herbs are laid on top in transit to ward off spirits, says how seriously it is taken.
